pull.title: BIP-379: add test vectors from rust-miniscript
pull.body:
The BIP-379 currently has a `TBD` in the test vector section.
I have extracted a bunch of test vectors from the [`rust-miniscript`](https://github.com/rust-bitcoin/rust-miniscript/) project, either directly or by slightly modifying test code to dump them into text/TSV files.
They have been very helpful for re-implementation in another language, so I think they should be made easily available here.

labels.name: Proposed BIP modification
labels.description: PR by non-owner to update BIP content

events.body: Concept ACK. It may be handy to provide a file here that runs/verifies the test vectors.

> Concept ACK. It may be handy to provide a file here that runs/verifies the test vectors.

That's a great idea. I've added that in the latest push.
Output looks like this:

```shell
$ cd bip-0379; go run main.go
Checking the BIP379 test vectors in . against
github.com/btcsuite/btcd/descriptors/miniscript.

Testing vectors in valid_from_alloy.txt       [positive]: 5896/5896 done (type column not compared)
Testing vectors in valid_8f1e8_from_alloy.txt [positive]: 3492/3492 done (type column not compared)
Testing vectors in malleable_from_alloy.txt   [positive/negative]: 7024/7024 + 7024/7024 done
Testing vectors in conflict_from_alloy.txt    [positive]: 1773/1773 done (1586 of them are rejected by the sanity checks)
Testing vectors in edge_cases.txt             [positive]: 42/42 done
Testing vectors in opcodes.txt                [positive]: 18185/18185 done (type and op count columns not compared)
Testing vectors in invalid.txt                [negative]: 5574/5574 done
Testing vectors in props_from_rust.tsv        [positive]: 8198/8198 done (op_count and exec_stack columns not compared)
Testing vectors in props_from_rust_tap.tsv    [positive/negative]: 6728/6728 + 1470/1470 done (op_count and exec_stack columns not compared)
Testing vectors in scripts_from_rust.tsv      [positive]: 8198/8198 done
Testing vectors in scripts_from_rust_tap.tsv  [positive/negative]: 6728/6728 + 1470/1470 done
Testing vectors in redeem.json                [positive/negative]: 12/12 + 34/34 done (each spend is executed in the script engine)

All 81848 vectors passed (0 skipped).


```
cc Authors: @sipa, @apoelstra, @sanket1729, @darosior, @achow101

I tried to run these tests through the Bitcoin Core miniscript implementation, but quickly hit the problem that the typing rules are inplemented inconsistently. This isn't a problem in production, because the differences are all within expressions that are invalid (for the correctness-related typing rules) or malleable (for the malleability-related typing rules) anyway, but it does mean that exact type tests like the ones in `malleable_from_alloy.txt` enforce than strictly needed.

In fact, rust-miniscript, Bitcoin Core, and the BIP text are all inconsistent with each other, in minor irrelevant ways. If we want to go the direction of having strict test vectors (which I support), I think we also need to first align all implementations and specifications. My suggestion would be to make everything match the BIP text. I have an (LLM written) patch for Bitcoin Core to make it do that (which passes all its unit & fuzz tests) which I'm happy to PR, but someone else will need to do the same for rust-bitcoin. It differs from the BIP in one rule: the `thresh` rule for the "unique dissatisfiable" `e` rule in the BIP is that all children are `s`, while rust-miniscript (and Bitcoin Core, so far) additionally (and superfluously) require that all children are `e`.

> My suggestion would be to make everything match the BIP text.

(non-author) approach ACK

Thanks a lot for testing the test vectors with Bitcoin Core, @sipa.

I'm also in favor of attempting to align everything with the BIP text.

> but someone else will need to do the same for rust-bitcoin

Will attempt that soon-ish.

EDIT: Here's the [BIP amendment PR](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/pull/2267) and the [`rust-miniscript` PR](https://github.com/rust-bitcoin/rust-miniscript/pull/1032).
I I've pushed up a fixup commit (3526e43) that addresses https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/pull/2240#issuecomment-5347499382 (and also fixes the Golang import issues I didn't realize were there).

concept ACK. Great effort. I'm sure a LLM can fill in the documented gaps in a followup PR.

I didn't look at the test vectors or the Go code, but the markdown updates look good to me.

Will review https://github.com/rust-bitcoin/rust-miniscript/pull/1032 more carefully.

I've updated the test vectors in a fixup commit to match the discussion in https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/pull/2267 and the proposed changes in https://github.com/rust-bitcoin/rust-miniscript/pull/1037.

events.body: Thanks for the reviews and updates to the implementations, great to see that y’all are on it.

The harness compares sat_witness_elements and sat_size, and both count as rust-miniscript does. The BIP does not say what they count. An implementation that counts as Bitcoin Core does fails every sat_witness_elements row and 21% of sat_size rows.

I ran the vectors at 47047eb through btclib-wallet's miniscript module, which reproduces the resource numbers in Core's miniscript_tests.cpp. Once malleable expressions carry no "s", "f" or "e", as #2267 says, it agrees on every row for validity, types, timelock mixing, malleability, requires_sig, script_size and both script tables. It also disagrees on 10% of the opcodes.txt ops and on op_count and exec_stack, none of which the harness compares.

Two examples. `pk(A)` has sat_witness_elements 2 where Core counts 1: the vector counts the witness script, which the BIP's 100-element rule excludes. In the Tapscript table, `thresh(1,pk(A),s:pk(B))` has sat_size 132, two 66-byte signatures, and no valid witness is that large. Two valid signatures make the count 2, not 1. Under BIP342 a failed non-empty signature fails the script, so the key that does not sign gives an empty signature. The largest witness is then 67, which is what Core gives. Other differences come from dissatisfactions Core does not count, such as a hash's.

Could the Files table say what each of these columns counts, or could the harness skip sat_witness_elements and sat_size as it does op_count and exec_stack?

Thanks for running the vectors against `btclib`, that's very useful independent validation.

There were two separate issues:

- **`thresh` was a bug.** The extraction sized k+1 satisfied sub expressions instead of k (fixed upstream in rust-bitcoin/rust-miniscript#1040). The regenerated tables now give 67 for `thresh(1,pk(A),s:pk(B))`, the same as you got.
- **The rest is how the columns are counted.** They follow `rust-miniscript`: `sat_witness_elements` adds one for the witness script, and `op_count` / `sat_size` maximize over all satisfactions, malleable ones included. Core never dissatisfies a hash fragment. Changing only that rule in the Go implementation reproduces your figures: 9.6% of `opcodes.txt` ops and 20–22% of `sat_size` rows.

I went with your first suggestion and updated the PR:

- A new "Resource Columns" section defines each column and states the difference from Core. `exec_stack` and the Tapscript `op_count` are marked informative only.
- New `limits[_tap].txt` has within/over vectors at each limit (201 ops, 3,600 bytes, 100 witness elements, 1,000 Tapscript stack elements), with no hash fragments. Core and the Go implementation agree on all ten verdicts. `rust-miniscript` rejects the 100-element `within` vector, because it counts the witness script against that limit.
- The harness now compares types, op counts and the limit verdicts. It skips only `exec_stack` and the Tapscript `op_count`.
- Everything now comes from unmodified `rust-miniscript` master (`698b97f`).

ACK 217afc1416d1d51f97ac3c3b1c70a306ce7ce242

I ran the vectors through btclib-wallet's miniscript module (not redeem.json, and not the Go harness). Parsing, types, scripts and the ten limit verdicts agree. The resource columns differ only by the two rules the new section describes, apart from `exec_stack` and the Tapscript `op_count`, which the section already sets aside.

Two wording nits. The Files table says every line of `conflict_from_alloy.txt` mixes timelock kinds on one path, but 187 of the 1,773 do not, for example `and_v(v:multi(2,A,B,C),andor(multi(2,D,E,F),after(500000001),after(1)))`, which `props_from_rust.tsv` marks `mixed_timelocks=false`. And `edge_cases.txt` is not "the only hand-written file": `limits.txt` and `limits_tap.txt` are too.
Thanks for the feedback, @fametrano! I've updated the text to fix the nits you mentioned.

reACK c923f2e961c0bae99a7b777cc15bb91601ed3bd9

Only `bip-0379.md` and `main.go` changed since 217afc1, and the vector files are identical, so my earlier run still holds. Both nits are fixed, and the new `conflictInsane = 1586` is the 1,773 lines minus the 187 sane ones I found.

concept ACK from me

reACK 91fdd5d3aa9e9131c4109cf84891241d8dce7f3a

Only `go.mod` and `go.sum` changed since c923f2e. The vectors, `main.go` and `bip-0379.md` are identical, so my earlier run still holds.

I would go out on a limb here and say that this can probably be merged independently.

The main discussion item of this PR (the type of malleable expressions) was resolved by #2267, and the vectors follow that. They agree with the current BIP text and with `rust-miniscript@698b97f` (apart from the one `limits.txt` vector it rejects, as documented in Provenance).

Bitcoin Core still reports `s`, `f` and `e` on malleable expressions. Once those are dropped, as #2267 says an API should, Core agrees with every type in the vectors, so this is not a bug and can be handled in the test code.
[Pieter's PR](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36028) is independent of that. It makes Core's typing rules match the BIP's tables literally, but with that rule applied it doesn't change Core's results on these vectors. So neither PR has to wait for the other.

EDIT: corrected the part about bitcoin/bitcoin#36028 after running the test vectors through Core. Added the cross-check table(s).

<details>

<summary>Cross-check between different implementations (LLM-generated)</summary>

## Summary

* All three implementations agree with every vector on parsing and rejection, sanity,
  timelock mixing, `script_size`, `non_malleable`, `requires_sig`, the script encoding
  in both contexts, and the `redeem.json` spends. The only exception is one limit
  vector in rust-miniscript (item 6 below).
* Bitcoin Core and btclib-wallet produce identical values for every resource column,
  and so they fail on exactly the same rows. Every one of those rows is a difference in
  how a quantity is counted, and the BIP text already describes it. No vector is wrong.
* Bitcoin Core also reports `s`, `f` and `e` on malleable expressions. The vectors
  leave them out, as #2267 asks of APIs. Once Core's types drop them, Core and
  btclib-wallet fail exactly the same 16,573 vectors, with the same values.
* bitcoin/bitcoin#36028 doesn't change any of this. Applied on current master, it
  leaves the results identical once `s`/`f`/`e` are dropped. Comparing raw types, it
  adds 558 failures. Details are under item 1.

## What was compared

| Source | Version |
|---|---|
| Test vectors | this PR, `91fdd5d3` |
| BIP text | this PR, `91fdd5d3` |
| rust-miniscript | `698b97f`, the commit named in Provenance |
| Bitcoin Core | master `a527a0077a0f`, and the same with bitcoin/bitcoin#36028 (`2631ece7b5`) applied on top |
| btclib-wallet | `cab4c7b` (main) |

Each implementation read every expression with its own parser, with the keys
substituted as the Conventions section describes. These were the checks:

* **Types:** compared as sorted letters.
* **Resource columns:** every column of `props_from_rust[_tap].tsv` and the `<ops>` of
  `opcodes.txt` were compared exactly, `exec_stack` and the Tapscript `op_count`
  included.
* **Limit vectors:** a `within` vector has to parse as sane, and an `over` vector has to
  be rejected.
* **`redeem.json`:** each implementation built the witness with its own non-malleable
  satisfier, signed with `SIGHASH_ALL`, and the spend of the P2WSH output was executed.
  rust-miniscript used libbitcoinconsensus, Bitcoin Core its own interpreter with the
  standard flags, and btclib-wallet its own script engine.

## Results per file

A ✓ means every vector of the file passes. Otherwise the cell gives the number of
failing vectors.

| File | Vectors | rust-miniscript | Core | Core + #36028 | btclib-wallet |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `valid_from_alloy.txt` | 5,896 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `valid_8f1e8_from_alloy.txt` | 3,492 | ✓ | 1,732 (type) | 2,070 (type) | ✓ |
| `malleable_from_alloy.txt` | 7,024 + 7,024 not sane | ✓ | 7,024 (type) | 7,024 (type) | ✓ |
| `conflict_from_alloy.txt` | 1,773 + 1,586 not sane | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `edge_cases.txt` | 42 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `opcodes.txt` | 18,185 | ✓ | 9,192 (8,756 type, 1,741 ops) | 9,412 | 1,741 (ops) |
| `invalid.txt` | 5,574 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `limits.txt` | 8 | 1 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `limits_tap.txt` | 2 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `props_from_rust.tsv` | 8,198 | ✓ | 8,151 | 8,151 | 8,151 |
| `props_from_rust_tap.tsv` | 6,728 + 1,470 `PARSE_ERR` | ✓ | 6,681 | 6,681 | 6,681 |
| `scripts_from_rust.tsv` | 8,198 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `scripts_from_rust_tap.tsv` | 6,728 + 1,470 `ERR` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `redeem.json` | 12 + 34 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Failing, of 81,860** | | **1** | **32,780** | **33,338** | **16,573** |

Here is what makes the props rows fail, counted per column. Core (with or without
#36028) and btclib-wallet have the same counts:

| Column | `props_from_rust.tsv` | `props_from_rust_tap.tsv` | Cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| `op_count` | 691 (8.4%) | 5,004 (4,883 `multi_a` + 121 hash) | items 4 and 5 |
| `sat_witness_elements` (after adding one, see item 3) | 1,345 (16.4%) | 1,209 (18.0%) | item 4 |
| `sat_size` | 1,623 (19.8%) | 1,474 (21.9%) | item 4 |
| `exec_stack` | 8,015 | 6,660 | item 5 |
| everything else | 0 | 0 | |

## Differences

| # | Topic | Vectors and BIP text | rust-miniscript | Bitcoin Core | btclib-wallet | Proposed resolution |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `s`/`f`/`e` in the type of a malleable expression | left out; the BIP says an API should report them false | left out | reports them | left out | **Core:** drop them when comparing against the vectors. **BIP:** say so in Conventions. |
| 2 | `sat_witness_elements` counts the witness script | yes, "plus one" | yes | no | no | **BIP:** explain why the column is one higher, and that such implementations compare their count plus one. |
| 3 | Malleable satisfactions in `op_count`, `sat_witness_elements` and `sat_size` | counted, as the BIP describes | counted | not counted | not counted | **BIP:** make the summary sentence say exactly which columns agree. |
| 4 | Tapscript `op_count` of `multi_a` | 0; the BIP says the column has no meaning | 0 | counts the opcodes | counts the opcodes | **BIP:** name the difference. Don't compare this column. |
| 5 | `exec_stack` | rust-miniscript's estimate, as the BIP describes | same | peak stack size including the witness | same as Core | **BIP:** name what Core reports instead. Don't compare this column. |
| 6 | `limits.txt` `witness_elements` `within` | 100 elements, the witness script excluded | rejects it | accepts it | accepts it | **rust-miniscript:** fix the off-by-one. The existing note in Provenance stays until then. |

### 1. `s`, `f` and `e` on malleable expressions, and bitcoin/bitcoin#36028

#2267, which was merged, added this to the Malleability section: *"Implementors of APIs
which unconditionally return values for these properties should always return false
for malleable expressions."* The vectors follow it, and so do rust-miniscript (since
rust-bitcoin/rust-miniscript#1037) and btclib-wallet. Bitcoin Core's type computation
still reports these letters on malleable expressions. For example,
`andor(jc:pk_k(A),after(500000001),0)` has type `doB` in the vectors, but Core reports
`Bodes`. That accounts for every type failure in Core: 1,732 lines of
`valid_8f1e8_from_alloy.txt`, all 7,024 of `malleable_from_alloy.txt` and 8,756 of
`opcodes.txt`. Once Core's type drops `s`, `f` and `e` whenever `m` is absent, Core
agrees with every type in every file.

bitcoin/bitcoin#36028 applies cleanly to current master, and Core's own
`miniscript_tests` still pass with it. It changes four rules to match the BIP's tables
literally:
* `d:` always gets `o` and `e`;
* `or_b` always gets `e`;
* `thresh` gets `e` when all its children are `s`.

Each of these changes only the type of an expression that is invalid or malleable
anyway. On the vectors:

* **Comparing raw types**, Core with #36028 fails *more* vectors: 33,338 instead of
  32,780. All 249 expressions whose type changes are malleable, and they all gain an
  `e` that the vectors leave out. For example,
  `and_b(multi(2,A,B,C),a:or_b(j:multi(2,D,E,F),a:multi(2,G,I,J)))` goes from `Bndus`
  to `Bndues`, while the vectors say `Bdnu`.
* **With `s`/`f`/`e` dropped from malleable types**, Core produces exactly the same
  results with and without #36028.

So #36028 neither resolves nor causes any difference with the vectors. What makes Core
agree is the rule from #2267 (malleable means no `s`, `f` or `e`). This can be applied
in Core's test code, as sipa suggested in #2267 ("the actual logic implementing this
can be pushed to the tests, so no internal code changes are needed"), or in Core's
type accessor. #36028 is still useful on its own merits, because it makes Core's raw
typing rules read like the BIP's tables. But this PR doesn't need to wait for it.

### 2. `sat_witness_elements` is one higher than Core's count

The column is rust-miniscript's `max_satisfaction_witness_elements`. It counts the
witness script as one of the witness elements, in both contexts. Core's
`GetStackSize()` and btclib-wallet's `max_stack_items` count only the elements that
satisfy the script, which is also the number the 100-element P2WSH standardness limit
applies to. For `pk(A)`, the witness is `<sig> <script>`, so the column says 2, while
Core and btclib-wallet say 1.

So every row that has a satisfaction is exactly one higher than Core's value. An
implementation that counts like Core has to add one to its own count before comparing.
The BIP already says "plus one", but not why, or what such an implementation should do;
the proposed wording adds both. After adding one, the rows that still differ are the
ones described in item 3.

### 3. Malleable satisfactions in `op_count`, `sat_witness_elements` and `sat_size`

As the Resource Columns section says, these columns are the maximum over every
satisfaction the fragment rules allow, malleable ones included. One such satisfaction
dissatisfies a hash fragment with a 32-byte value that is not the preimage. Core and
btclib-wallet count only non-malleable satisfactions, and those never dissatisfy a hash
fragment. Every differing row contains a hash fragment, Core and btclib-wallet are
always the lower value, and the two agree with each other in every row.

* **`opcodes.txt`:** `or_d(c:pk_k(A),or_d(sha256(926a…),multi(2,B,C,D)))` has `<ops>`
  15, but Core and btclib-wallet say 12. The vectors count the path that dissatisfies
  `pk_k(A)` and `sha256`, then executes the `CHECKMULTISIG` with its 3 keys. Without
  dissatisfying `sha256`, `multi` is never reached.
* **`props_from_rust.tsv`:** `or_b(sha256(926a…),ac:pk_k(A))` has `sat_size` 106, a
  73-byte signature plus 33 bytes of non-preimage. Core and btclib-wallet say 34, the
  33-byte preimage plus an empty dissatisfaction of `pk_k(A)`.

The rates match what the BIP says ("roughly one in ten op counts and one in five
`sat_size` values"):
* op counts: 8.4% of `props_from_rust.tsv` and 9.6% of `opcodes.txt`;
* `sat_size`: 19.8% and 21.9%.

The one sentence I'd change is "an implementation that counts like Core reproduces
every other column". It doesn't hold for `exec_stack` or for the Tapscript `op_count`
(items 4 and 5). It also doesn't say that `sat_witness_elements` keeps differing in
these rows after adding one (16.4% and 18.0%).

### 4. Tapscript `op_count`

The column counts a `multi_a` as no ops at all, and the BIP already says the column has
no meaning in Tapscript. Core and btclib-wallet count its opcodes: `multi_a(1,A)` is 0
in the vectors and 2 in both of them. That accounts for 4,883 rows. The remaining 121
rows of the 5,004 are the hash-fragment rows of item 3. `main.go` already skips this
column, and other implementations should skip it too.

### 5. `exec_stack`

The column is rust-miniscript's estimate of how many elements the script pushes above
its witness, and the BIP says so. Core's `GetExecStackSize()` and btclib-wallet's
`max_exec_stack_items` report the peak stack size during execution, witness elements
included, which is what the 1,000-element limit bounds. For example,
`and_b(after(1),a:and_b(after(1),ac:pk_k(A)))` is 3 in the vectors and 4 in both of
them. No offset maps one quantity onto the other: even after subtracting the witness
elements, the difference ranges from −2 to +2 in P2WSH and from −4 to 0 in Tapscript.
`main.go` already skips this column, and other implementations should skip it too.

### 6. rust-miniscript rejects the `witness_elements` `within` vector

In `limits.txt`, `within` is a chain of `and_v(v:pk(K1),…)` with 100 keys, so its
satisfaction has 100 elements. `over` has 101 keys. The BIP's Resource Limits section,
like Core's policy, excludes the witness script from the 100-element limit. However,
rust-miniscript's `Segwitv0::check_local_policy_validity` compares
`max_satisfaction_witness_elements()`, which includes the script, against 100. It
therefore rejects a satisfaction with exactly 100 elements. The code is unchanged on
current master (`d57bb31`). Core and btclib-wallet accept `within` and reject `over`.
The vector is correct, and the BIP already documents this behaviour in Provenance. The
fix belongs in rust-miniscript: compare the count minus one.

</details>

> Cross-check between different implementations (LLM-generated)

For finding 2 (rust-miniscript `max_satisfaction_witness_elements` counts the witness script as a witness element) the bot proposes just documenting the difference.

But I think we should fix rust-miniscript to not count the witness script.

Finding 6 is related (when checking limits, rust-miniscript counts the witness script against the 100 limit), and there the bot suggests fixing rust-miniscript, which I agree with.

Both of these seem to stem from the same confusion on my part about whether the witness script counts as a witness element.

The other four findings I agree are uninteresting and (at most) just need a mention that the implementations differ.
Okay, thanks for the explanation. Sounds like this is ready to go.
I noticed that BIP379: Miniscript was still in Draft status, but clearly multiple implementations support it on Mainnet. I therefore created a follow-up to advance it to Deployed in #2359.
